problem: Visual navigation policies are trained for a single environment; training one policy across several environment types is slow, and a jointly trained baseline is weaker, while separately trained experts fail outside their own environment.
motivation: Humans change behaviour with the environment (careful in a china shop, fast in an empty hallway), so robots operating in many environments should too. A single model should share knowledge across environments while keeping environment-specific behaviour.
key_idea: Treat multi-environment navigation as multi-task RL: a Siamese feature extractor feeds several expert actor-critic networks that are softly blended by an attention gate, and an auxiliary environment (room) classifier regularizes the shared features.
insight: Joint-training and expert baselines show that blending experts gives both cross-environment sharing and specialization. MERLIN beats the specialists in most of their own environments and converges 24-26% faster than the joint expert. The gap to the joint expert grows in the largest environments (Env1 in simulation, Env7 in the real data). The paper attributes the faster convergence to the classification loss, but there is no separate ablation removing the classifier or the attention gate.
method: Siamese feature extractor: shared-weight CNN on the current view and the target view, each normalized and concatenated into a state embedding; it is trained by both the RL loss and the classifier loss.
Expert sub-networks: n actor-critic networks (n = number of environments), each with the Zhu et al. target-driven backbone, a softmax policy head and a linear value head.
Attentive soft blending: an attention network gives softmax weights over experts; the final policy and value are weighted sums of the experts' action distributions and values.
Environment (Room) Classifier: an auxiliary supervised branch predicting the environment label from the features; its loss updates only the RC network and the feature extractor.

Training: multi-thread A3C over 4 simulated (AI2-THOR) or 3 real (Turtlebot images) gridded environments simultaneously; the reward is a step penalty plus a collision penalty, with a terminal bonus or penalty at the step limit.

setting.backbone: Siamese CNN + n expert actor-critic networks (Zhu et al. target-driven architecture) + attention gate + room classifier, trained from scratch with A3C
setting.training_data: Online RL in 4 AI2-THOR simulated rooms (kitchen, living room, bathroom, tiny bathroom) and 3 real environments (living room, common room, corridor) captured with a Turtlebot as gridded image sets; no extra data
setting.observation: monocular RGB of the current view and the target view
setting.action_space: discrete: step forward, step backward, turn left/right 90° on a square grid
setting.simulator: AI2-THOR (gridded); real-world image dataset trained off-line; Turtlebot live demo
setting.privileged: none at test time (environment labels are used only in training for the classifier)

numbers_note: The benchmarks are custom (AI2-THOR gridded rooms and a self-collected real dataset), not canonical navigation benchmarks. Tables report episode length and reach-goal %, not standard metrics, so numbers are omitted. Sim table: MERLIN avg episode length 12.38, avg reach goal 99.50%, RC accuracy 99.61%, converges in 23K steps (Joint Expert 14.30, 99.30%, 31K). Real table: MERLIN 25.35, 94.60%, 19K steps (Joint Expert 26.28, 94.10%, 25K).
results: On the simulated rooms, MERLIN reaches 99.50% success with average episode length 12.38, versus the joint expert's 14.30 and 99.30%, and converges in 23K steps versus 31K. On the real data it reaches 94.60% with length 25.35 versus 94.10% and 26.28, at 19K versus 25K steps. It stays above 80% success up to noise equal to 100% of the grid size and beats the joint expert throughout. A live Turtlebot demo in the corridor succeeds with minor missteps.
limitations: Evaluation is on small, custom, gridded environments (4 simulated, 3 real) with discrete 90° turns; the model has trouble with inaccurate turning angles and drift on the real robot.
The number of experts equals the number of environments, and the classifier needs supervised environment labels, so it cannot handle unseen environment types.
No ablation isolates the classifier or the attention gate, and there is no comparison beyond Zhu et al. baselines.
compares_to: Zhu et al. target-driven navigation (per-environment experts)
Zhu et al. jointly trained (Joint Expert)
